memory_support.text: Signal decides flex direction; two plus rides free; dotted entry only.

claim.text: Common mistake, labelled as a misconception: you may cross a double white line whenever traffic looks clear.

correction.text: Crossing a double white line to enter or leave the express lane is prohibited; use only dotted-line access points.

answer.text: Only at dotted-line access points; crossing the double white line is prohibited.

prompt.text: A driver wants to slip into the express lane across a solid double white marking. Is that allowed, and where is movement allowed?

rationale.text: The double white line bars crossing, so entry and exit are limited to dotted-line access points.

lines.text: Flex lanes can reverse direction by time of day.
Check overhead signal before entering lane.

narration.text: Welcome to freeway, flex and express lane driving. Flex lanes may reverse direction by time of day, so the overhead signal controls whether you may enter. On the freeway you also keep at least two seconds of following distance, and you lengthen that gap when conditions worsen. These two habits set up everything else in this session, because lane choice and space protect you when speeds are high and traffic is dense.

lines.text: Keep at least two seconds behind ahead vehicle.
Lengthen gap when conditions worsen.
Move safely right when faster traffic approaches behind.

narration.text: Keep at least two seconds of following distance on the freeway, and make that gap larger when rain, fog, heavy traffic or other poor conditions reduce control. A left-lane driver who is approached from behind must move safely right so faster traffic can pass. Lingering in the left lane can draw a citation for impeding, and it forces others into risky passes. Space plus courtesy keeps freeway flow smooth and lawful.

lines.text: Freeway turnarounds are prohibited entirely.
Never drive or stop for passengers outside solid white line.
Use runaway ramps only for emergency stops.

narration.text: U-turns on the freeway are prohibited, and you must not drive in the emergency lane outside the solid white line or stop there for passengers. That outer lane is for emergency use only. In the same spirit, runaway-vehicle ramps are for emergency stops only, and stopping, standing or parking on one or in its path is prohibited. These places look empty, but blocking them removes a lifesaving escape for someone else.

lines.text: Two or more occupants ride express free.
Motorcycles, buses and registered clean-fuel decal vehicles ride free.
Enter or exit only at dotted-line access points.

narration.text: Express lanes on I-15 are free for vehicles with two or more occupants, plus motorcycles, buses and registered clean-fuel decal vehicles. Even when you qualify, crossing a double white line to enter or leave the express lane is prohibited. You may enter or exit only at dotted-line access points. Waiting for the dotted opening keeps you from cutting across a barrier that separates fast toll traffic from general lanes.

lines.text: Meters alternate red and green for ramp traffic.
They release generally one vehicle per green.
Obey only when meter-on sign is lit.

narration.text: Ramp meters show alternating red and green and generally release one vehicle per green. You obey the meter only when the meter-on sign is lit; when it is dark you enter as usual. At a single-point interchange, a U-turn from the off-ramp that re-enters the freeway is allowed only when you face a green arrow, and you must finish once started. Both rules ask you to obey the light that controls your exact movement.

lines.text: Passenger count never authorizes crossing double white line.
Even qualifying cars must wait for dotted access.

narration.text: Here is the trap that confuses many drivers. You carry three friends, so you qualify to ride free, and the express lane looks open. You might think a full car can cross the double white line anywhere. That is wrong. Qualifying occupancy decides toll-free use, but only dotted-line access points decide where you may move in or out. Crossing the double white line remains prohibited even for qualified vehicles.

lines.text: Recall where express entry is allowed.
Consider why double white bars crossing.

narration.text: Pause and test yourself. A driver wants to slip into the express lane across a solid double white marking. Is that allowed, and where is movement allowed. The answer is that it is not allowed there. Entry and exit are allowed only at dotted-line access points, because crossing the double white line is prohibited. Hold that distinction between who may ride and where you may enter.

lines.text: Check signals, keep gap, respect lane limits.
Obey meters and green-arrow turnarounds.

narration.text: To close, remember the freeway pattern. Check the overhead signal before a flex lane, keep at least two seconds and more when conditions worsen, never turn around or misuse the emergency lane, move right for faster traffic, use express lanes only when qualified and only at dotted access, obey ramp meters when lit, keep runaway ramps clear, and make the single-point turnaround only on a green arrow and finish once started.

why_how.text: Flex lanes reverse by time of day, so the overhead signal tells whether the lane is open right now.
A two-second gap that grows in poor conditions gives stopping room, while moving right for faster traffic prevents impeding and citations.
Occupancy decides who rides express free, while the double white line decides where movement may occur, so qualification never overrides the dotted-access rule.

reasoning.text: The car has two occupants so toll-free use is allowed, but the lane edge is a double white line with no dotted opening yet.

result.text: The driver continues in the general lane and enters only when a dotted-line access point appears.

scenario.text: A driver with one passenger approaches the express lane and sees a continuous double white line.

memory_support.text: Slow scan assume nothing; stop behind see tires; first there goes first.

claim.text: A myth, labelled as a misconception: at a tied four-way stop the driver on the left goes first.

correction.text: Grant the way to the driver on the right at a tied four-way stop, to oncoming traffic on a left turn, and to the vehicle already in the intersection.

answer.text: Yield to the driver on the right, to oncoming traffic when turning left, and to anyone already inside.

prompt.text: You and another car reach a four-way stop together, and you plan to turn left across their path. Who moves first and why?

rationale.text: The tied stop favors the driver on the right, and a left turn yields to oncoming traffic, so you wait in this case.

lines.text: Slow and scan every intersection approach.
Never assume others will yield.

narration.text: Every intersection asks for the same opening habit. Slow down, scan for controls, cross traffic, walkers, riders and sight blocks, and never assume others will yield. Right-of-way rules then decide who moves first, including the vehicle already inside, oncoming traffic on a left turn, the driver on the right at a tied four-way stop, and road traffic when you leave a drive. Scanning plus yielding prevents the most common crossing crashes.

lines.text: Stop fully behind signs, signals and stop lines.
In queues leave room to see rear tires ahead.
Yield in any crosswalk, marked or not.

narration.text: Stop fully behind signs, signals, walks or stop lines, and when queued leave room to see the rear tires of the vehicle ahead. That space gives you an escape path and prevents crowding the crossing. At signs and signals you also stop behind the stop line or crosswalk and grant passage to anyone in or entering any crosswalk, marked or not. Paint does not create the duty; the presence of a walker does.

lines.text: Broken yellow permits passing when safe.
Solid and double-center lines restrict as marked.
Enter shared center lane within five hundred feet only.

narration.text: Broken yellow center lines permit passing when safe, while solid lines and double-center lines restrict or bar passing as marked. The pattern tells you what is allowed, not just the color. For the shared center left-turn lane, enter no more than five hundred feet before the turn, after mirrors, signal and blind-spot check. Late entry after checks keeps the shared lane for turning rather than cruising or passing.

lines.text: Twenty near schools, twenty-five in neighborhoods and business areas.
Fifty-five on major highways as posted.
Reduce speed where sight or control shrinks.

narration.text: When no signs or hazards change them, default limits are twenty near schools during recess or arrival and dismissal, twenty-five in business and residential areas, and fifty-five on major highways as posted. Beyond those numbers, reduce speed at intersections, rail crossings, curves, hill crests, narrow or winding roads, work zones and whenever sight or control is reduced. Lawful speed means the posted default adjusted down for real hazards.

lines.text: Steady yellow warns red is near.
Flashing yellow arrow needs yield before turning.
Right on red needs full stop; red arrow means wait.

narration.text: Signals bridge perception to action. Steady yellow means the signal is about to turn red, while flashing yellow means slow, proceed with care and be ready to stop. A flashing yellow arrow permits the turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and walkers, who hold the green. Right on red is allowed after a full stop unless posted otherwise, but right or left on a red arrow requires waiting for a go indication. Yield first, then go.

lines.text: Tied stop favors driver on your right.
Left turn yields to oncoming traffic.

narration.text: Now check your grasp of priority. You and another car reach a four-way stop together, and you plan to turn left across their path. Who moves first and why. You wait. The tied stop favors the driver on the right, and a left turn yields to oncoming traffic. The vehicle already in the intersection also goes before you, and road traffic goes before a driver leaving a drive. Never claim priority; yield it.

lines.text: Roundabouts need slow yield enter exit routine.
Orange diamonds mean work zone, fines doubled.

narration.text: To finish, link the remaining street skills. For roundabouts, slow on approach, yield to traffic inside and to walkers, enter when clear, then exit at the wanted street. At rail tracks, cross promptly without stopping on them, and wait until arms rise and lights end before going. Warning signs are generally diamond-shaped yellow with black symbols, guide signs are square or rectangular green, brown or blue, and work-zone signs are orange with doubled speeding fines.

why_how.text: Scanning every approach matters because others may not yield, so priority goes to prior arrival, oncoming traffic on left turns, and the right-side tie.
Stopping behind the line preserves sight and walk space, which is why crosswalk duty applies even when no paint marks the crossing.
Defaults set a baseline by area, while hazard slowing adjusts for reduced sight or control at curves, crests, crossings and work zones.

reasoning.text: Both cars arrive together so the tie rule applies, and the planned left turn adds a yield to oncoming traffic.

result.text: The driver waits, lets the car on the right and any oncoming traffic clear, then turns when the path is safe.

scenario.text: A driver reaches a four-way stop at the same moment as the car on the right and wants to turn left.

memory_support.text: Green clear yellow caution; red waits officer rules.

claim.text: Wrong and labelled as a misconception: green always means go without looking, and signals outrank an officer.

correction.text: Green means go only if clear, yellow warns red is near, and an officer directing traffic overrides any signal.

answer.text: Stop and wait, allow right on red after stop unless barred, honor red arrows, obey the officer, and stop first at a dead signal.

prompt.text: Your light is green but an officer waves you to stop, and later you face a dark dead signal. What do you do in each case?

rationale.text: The officer overrides the green so you stop, and a dead signal needs a full stop first with yield to the vehicle on the right unless directed otherwise.

lines.text: Green arrow open, red cross closed.
Overhead signal controls flex use.

narration.text: This spine ties special lanes together. Flex-lane use follows the overhead signal, with green arrow open and red cross closed. Express lanes need qualifying occupancy, and double white line crossing is barred except at dotted access points. Single-occupant use needs a paid pass account, while a clean-fuel decal is a separate windshield authorization. Signals plus authorization decide lawful lane use.

lines.text: Keep following gap, no turnaround.
No emergency-lane driving, no ramp reversal.
Approached left-lane car must move right.

narration.text: On the freeway keep the following gap, make no U-turn, do no emergency-lane driving and make no ramp reversal. A left-lane vehicle approached from behind must move right to avoid impeding. Use the acceleration lane to match speed, exit early and steady, and at a metered ramp go one vehicle per green. Each rule keeps high-speed merges orderly and prevents sudden blocks in fast traffic.

lines.text: Runaway ramps emergency only, no stopping.
Turnaround only on green arrow, finish once started.
Follow staged signals and lane guides.

narration.text: Runaway ramps are emergency-only with no stopping, and the single-point off-ramp U-turn is allowed on green arrow with never stopping mid-crossing. For continuous-flow, diverging-diamond and thru-U-turn layouts, each redirects lefts, so follow staged signals and lane guides. These interchanges look strange at first, but the staged lights and marked lanes walk you through each redirected turn safely.

lines.text: Approach slow and scan fully.
Stop behind line, look left-right-left, hold lane.

narration.text: Approach slow and scan, stop behind the line, look left-right-left, cross without lane change, then merge right. That step order keeps you placed and visible through the crossing. Never assume priority. Yield to prior arrival, oncoming traffic on a left turn, the right-side tie, driveway entrants, ramp traffic and anyone still inside. Procedure plus humility makes intersections predictable for everyone.

lines.text: Yellow divides opposing flow, white same direction.
Stop behind line, yield in crosswalk, limit center entry.
Reasonable speed, slow for hazards, never impede.

narration.text: Yellow divides opposing flow while white divides same-direction flow. Stop behind the line and yield in the crosswalk, with shared center lane entry limited before the turn. The basic speed law is reasonable and prudent, with posted defaults by area, slowing for hazards, and no driving so slowly that you impede traffic in a citable way. Markings show position, speed shows judgment, and both demand obedience.

lines.text: Green go if clear, arrow only arrow direction.
Yellow about to red, flashing yellow caution.
Orange work zones double fines, obey flaggers.

narration.text: Green means go if clear, green arrow allows only the arrow direction after yielding, yellow warns red is near, and flashing yellow means caution. For signs, guide informs, railroad crossings need caution and stop discipline, regulatory commands, warning diamonds alert, and work-zone orange brings doubled speeding fines with flagger obedience. Light and sign families each speak a different language you must answer correctly.

lines.text: Green still needs clear path check.
Officer orders beat any light.

narration.text: Here is a costly trap. You see green and want to surge through without looking, thinking green always means go. That is wrong. Green means go only if clear, after yielding to vehicles and walkers still inside. And if an officer orders a stop against your green, the officer overrides the signal. A second trap is treating flashing red like flashing yellow. Flashing red needs stop-then-go, while flashing yellow needs caution.

lines.text: Officer stop beats green light.
Dead signal needs stop first.

narration.text: Test the red and override rules. Your light is green but an officer waves you to stop, and later you face a dark dead signal. What do you do in each case. You stop for the officer even though you hold green, because the officer overrides the signal. At the dead signal you come to a full stop first, then yield before entering. Red means stop and wait, flashing red means stop-then-go, and red arrows mean stop until a go indication.

lines.text: Never assume, yield to prior arrival.
Yield on left, to right tie, from drive.

narration.text: Close with the habit that unites this spine. Never assume priority. Yield to prior arrival, oncoming traffic on a left turn, the right-side tie, driveway entrants, ramp traffic and anyone still inside. Carry that with lane discipline, intersection steps, marking obedience, reasonable speed, signal meanings and sign respect. Together those rules turn a confusing network of special lanes and novel interchanges into a predictable drive.

why_how.text: Occupancy plus dotted access plus pass or decal authorization together explain why a solo driver without authorization cannot ride free even at an open dotted entry.
Green allows movement only when the path is clear and after yielding, which is why yellow warns and red commands waiting, with officer orders on top.
Slow approach and triple look reveal hazards, while never assuming priority explains yields to prior arrival, oncoming left-turn traffic and right-side ties.

reasoning.text: Green would normally allow going, but the officer order overrides the signal and requires a stop.

result.text: The driver stops as directed and waits for the officer signal, then proceeds only when directed and clear.

scenario.text: A driver faces a green light while an officer in the intersection waves traffic to stop.
